structure.does: The story angle in news terms, specific and plain ('Data: 62% of UP wheat farmers sell within a week of harvest'); no 'Press release' or 'Collaboration'.
One sentence showing why this journalist: a recent piece of theirs this story extends or answers.
The news hook, why now, and why their readers care, in plain sentences.
The data, access or credentials that make it credible: numbers with their source and sample, who the spokesperson is, what is exclusive.
Exactly what you can provide and by when (interview slots, data set, photos, case-study contacts, exclusive until a date).
A simple ask ('Would this work for your agri coverage?'), then name, role, phone and one link.

length.note: Body words, excluding subject and signature. Shorter for reactive expert-comment pitches; longer only when the proof needs a few numbers. If it needs more, link a one-page brief.

checklist: Is the pitch addressed to one named journalist, with a reason they in particular should care?
Does the subject line state the story angle, not the company name or 'press release'?
Is the news hook (why now) in the first three sentences?
Is every number given with its source and sample?
Is the offer specific (who, what, by when, exclusive or not)?
Is the body under 250 words, with no attachments required to understand it?
Is it free of hype words ('revolutionary', 'game-changer') and generic greetings?
Are claims about competitors or people factual and attributable?
pitfalls: Data that falls apart on the first question: before pitching, have the sample size, method and dates ready; journalists check.
Offering the same 'exclusive' to three outlets: offer exclusives one at a time with a clear deadline, or call it what it is.
Pitching on the day of the event: features and data stories need lead time; reactive comments need speed. Match the timing to the story type.
Forgetting regional and Hindi media: for Bihar or UP stories, regional Hindi dailies and news creators may be the better first pitch; write the pitch in the outlet's language.

cards.name: Medical / regulatory writing
cards.summary: Scientific and regulatory documents for medicines, devices and clinical research: protocols, clinical study reports (CSRs), investigator brochures, regulatory submission summaries, patient information leaflets. Good medical writing follows the governing guideline and template exactly, states every result with its numbers, stays consistent with the source tables, and never claims more than the data support.
use_for: clinical study reports and synopses following ICH E3
protocols, informed consent forms and patient information sheets for ethics committees
regulatory submission summaries and responses to regulator queries (e.g. CDSCO in India)
plain-language summaries and patient leaflets
manuscripts and congress abstracts from trial data
avoid: Persuasive or promotional language in regulatory documents ('remarkable efficacy', 'breakthrough'): reviewers read it as bias. State the result, the comparison and the uncertainty.
Writing from memory or press summaries: every number must come from the client's tables, listings and figures (TLFs) or the cited source, and be traceable.
Consumer health marketing ('cures diabetes naturally'): that is advertising, governed by advertising law and codes; use the advertising genres and the health-claim compliance cards.
Ignoring the template: regulators and sponsors use fixed section numbering; a beautifully written document in the wrong structure gets sent back.

sources.title: ICH E3: Structure and Content of Clinical Study Reports (Step 4, 30 November 1995)
sources.supports: CSR sections 1-16 (title page, synopsis, ethics, investigators, introduction, objectives, investigational plan, study patients, efficacy, safety, discussion and conclusions, tables, references, appendices); synopsis 'usually limited to 3 pages' and 'should include numerical data to illustrate results, not just text or p-values'

hospitals and academic investigators running trials

cards.goal: The regulator, ethics committee, investigator or patient can find, verify and act on the information: approve, run the study correctly, or use the medicine safely.

structure.does: Before writing, name the guideline (ICH E3 for CSRs, ICH E6 for GCP documents, the regulator's own template) and the sponsor's SOP and style sheet; mirror their section numbering.
Product, protocol number, version, date, sponsor, confidentiality statement, as the template requires.

Objectives, design, population, endpoints, key efficacy and safety results with numbers (n, estimates, confidence intervals), and conclusions. ICH E3 expects numerical data, not only text or p-values.
structure.length: usually up to 3 pages for a CSR synopsis (ICH E3)

structure.does: For a CSR: ethics, investigators, introduction, objectives, investigational plan, study patients, efficacy, safety, discussion and conclusions (ICH E3 order). Each results statement cross-references its source table.
structure.length: per template; tens to hundreds of pages

structure.does: Interprets results against objectives, states limitations, and makes no claim beyond the data.
In-text tables matching the TLFs exactly, reference list, and appendices the guideline lists.
Plain-language summary or leaflet: what the medicine or study is, who it is for, how to use it, side effects in everyday words, what to do if something goes wrong.

length.note: Set by document type: a patient leaflet or plain-language summary is 1-4 pages, a CSR synopsis up to about 3 pages (ICH E3), a full CSR or submission module runs to hundreds of pages with appendices.

checklist: Does the document follow the governing guideline's or sponsor's template section by section?
Does every number match the source tables, listings or cited reference?
Are results reported with numbers (n, estimates, confidence intervals), not only p-values or adjectives?
Are terms, abbreviations, drug names and units consistent throughout and defined at first use?
Are safety findings reported as fully as efficacy findings?
Do conclusions stay within what the data show, with limitations stated?
Is it free of promotional language?
Has it had a quality-control check against source documents by someone other than the writer?
For patient-facing text: is it in plain language a patient can act on, in the language they read?
pitfalls: Copy-paste drift between synopsis and body: a number updated in one place and not the other is a classic query. Keep a single source table and check every repeat of each number.
Spin in conclusions (secondary endpoints promoted when the primary failed): report the primary endpoint first and plainly.

Patient documents written at clinician level: for informed consent and leaflets, test readability and translate properly (with back-translation) into Hindi and regional languages where participants need them.
AI-drafted text without verification: AI tools invent references and round numbers. Every statement must be checked against source data before QC.
cards.exemplar_brief: CSR synopsis in ICH E3 section-2 format for a completed phase III, 12-week, randomised, double-blind trial of a fixed-dose antihypertensive combination at 14 Indian sites (sponsor: a Hyderabad generic-pharma company), written only from the mock protocol and TLF summary below; audience: CDSCO reviewers and the sponsor's medical team; English; 900-1,400 words (within 3 pages) reporting efficacy and safety with numbers, confidence intervals and limitations; goal: a reviewer can verify every number against the tables. MOCK TLF SUMMARY (all numbers invented for this test): protocol HGP-AHT-301; first patient in Monday 12 January 2026, last patient last visit Monday 24 August 2026, database lock Monday 14 September 2026, report dated Wednesday 30 September 2026. Test: telmisartan 40 mg + amlodipine 5 mg once daily; comparator: telmisartan 40 mg once daily; adults with stage 2 essential hypertension. Table 14.1.1: randomised 216 / 214; completed 208 / 205 (discontinued 8 / 9: adverse event 3 / 4, lost to follow-up 3 / 2, consent withdrawn 2 / 3); full analysis and safety sets = all randomised. Baseline seated SBP 156.2 / 155.8 mmHg. Table 14.2.1 (primary, week 12, ANCOVA): LS-mean change in seated SBP -18.4 mmHg (95% CI -20.2 to -16.6) vs -12.1 (-13.9 to -10.3); difference -6.3 mmHg (95% CI -8.8 to -3.8). Table 14.3.1: TEAEs 61 (28.2%) / 52 (24.3%); SAEs 2 (0.9%) / 3 (1.4%), none drug-related; AE discontinuations 3 (1.4%) / 4 (1.9%). Top TEAEs: peripheral oedema 14 (6.5%) / 3 (1.4%); headache 11 (5.1%) / 12 (5.6%); dizziness 9 (4.2%) / 8 (3.7%). Limitations: 12 weeks, office BP only, no placebo arm.

verified.note: ROUND 2: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Complete ICH E3 section-2 synopsis in order, every number traceable to its named table, CIs on efficacy, safety reported as fully as efficacy, limitations stated, no promotional language, 1,009 words. All percentages recompute correctly from n/216 and n/214. Placeholders only where the brief gives nothing (sponsor name, investigators, planned n, inclusion thresholds, batch numbers). Nits (writer): 'the 6.3 mmHg difference does not come from an imbalance at the start' is interpretation beyond the TLFs (ANCOVA already adjusts); 'the AE discontinuations match the disposition table' is a QC note, not synopsis text; 'No hypothesis test is applied to the safety data' and 'Publication: None' are stated without a source. | round 1: weak 7
